docs.title: i. The AI Maturity Curve at work
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) introduces the Client Engineering Bob Marketplace and IBM Bob Demo-Builder Mode curriculum for hands-on enablement. [2 min]

Every seller has encountered the demo trade-off. A bespoke demonstration is persuasive, but consumes weeks of scarce technical talent. Alternatively, a canned demonstration is instant, but generic. Enterprise audiences will recognize the difference quickly.

IBM Bob Demo-Builder Mode is designed to collapse that trade-off. It scales expertise, rather than headcount: the method of IBM's best client engineers, captured once as a Mode, applied by any practitioner, on any opportunity, within a single working session.

The Demo-Builder Mode you will explore in the chapters ahead is a packaged Bob Custom Mode built and maintained by IBM Client Engineering. It captures the methodology applied by a senior solution engineer as a reusable asset. That asset carries a persona and a build lifecycle, together with decision gates and compliance guard-rails. It also carries the product knowledge required to embed IBM platforms into a real full-stack solution.

The outcome? A working, compliant, runnable client demonstration — produced in hours rather than weeks.

A core hallmark of the AI Maturity Curve is that IBM Bob always ensures that the user (you), the human-in-the-loop, maintains control and understanding throughout every interaction. The modules within the hands-on lab work ahead will further reinforce those notions: putting that maturity to work against the most valuable artifact in the pre-sales motion.

The graphic above serves as your map for this hands-on lab and the work ahead: register for IBM Bob; install the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder Mode (from the CE Bob Marketplace for IBMers or as a packaged download from Seismic for Business Partners); optionally configure the Carbon and TechZone MCP servers; and, from that point onward, you're ready to build. Notice that the asset types being wired together here— MCP servers for reach, a Mode for method —are the very extensibility concepts introduced within Module 4 | Scale & Extend. This lab is where those concepts will concretely come together into real-world, client-facing capabilities.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
The discipline you practiced in the IBM Bob Level 3 "Climbing the AI Maturity Curve" labs carries over into this content as well: Bob does the building; the human (you) ultimately keeps hands on the controls.

The Demo Builder asks crisp and targeted questions at genuine decision points — and works autonomously between them. Those decision points span use case identification and product fit, environment details and build path, and compliance.

WHAT IS THE AI MATURITY CURVE?

If this concept is new to you, the authors highly recommend checking out the IBM Bob Level 3 "Climbing the AI Maturity Curve" courseware. Many IBMers and Business Partners will have already taken this as part of their pre-requisite learning paths on generative AI coding assistants and IBM Bob. However, if you've missed it, there's no better time than the present to understanding how IBM Bob aligns with an enterprise organization's journey along the curve. The material and topics covered within the learning plan will greatly inform and enrich the concepts covered within the modules ahead.

The user remains in the decision seat the entire journey. What changes is the output: each session concludes with a demonstration you can place in front of a real-world client.

docs.title: iv. Before you start
docs.text:
Recall the closing note from Module 4 | Scale & Extend, which previewed a dedicated series of hands-on labs covering the IBM Bob Marketplace and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), as well as their synergies with IBM Technology Zone client-facing demonstrations. The hands-on work ahead assumes you have completed the core curriculum of that L3 course, or that you hold equivalent familiarity with the Bob IDE and the Agentic Sidebar as well as Custom Modes and MCP.

However, to simplify the work, your environment will begin as a fresh workspace. You will not need any code or repositories from the previous lab on your machine in order to complete the following lab. Nothing from the Galaxium Travels environment carries over into this one.

What you do need:

REQUIREMENTS

  • IBM Bob installed and authenticated — Chapter 1 has a registration page for each audience
  • Your IBMid credentials are at hand (IBM regular employees sign in with their w3id)
  • IBM regular employees: you can sign in to github.ibm.com and you are connected to the IBM Intranet (or via Cisco AnyConnect VPN)
  • Business Partners: you can reach IBM Seismic to download the packaged Demo Builder
  • A local folder is available to serve as your Bob project workspace

No additional downloads or staged files are required before you begin.

BUSINESS PARTNERS

Business Partners register for IBM Bob through IBM Technology Zone and follow their own Setup page, Business Partners | Setup and registration. That route is fully self-contained and requires neither github.ibm.com access nor an Intranet VPN connection.

docs.title: i. Overview
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Setup and registration curriculum for Bob Demo Builder hands-on enablement. [1 min]

This page is written for IBM regular employees. Business Partners should follow the companion page, Business Partners | Setup and registration, which registers through IBM Technology Zone and obtains the Demo Builder as a packaged download from Seismic.

Within this chapter, you will assemble the Bob Demo-Builder environment end-to-end:

  • Register for IBM Bob through the Internal registration route and authenticate the Bob IDE on your local machine
  • Install the Client Engineering (CE) Bob Marketplace extension via the Agentic Sidebar and create the GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) that unlocks its catalog
  • Install the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder collection into a fresh project workspace: the packaged Mode together with its Skills, Rules, and MCP configuration that the remainder of this lab runs upon
  • Verify the workspace, so that the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode is available within the Agentic Sidebar before any demo work begins
  • Optionally, acquire the short-lived credentials for (and configure) the Carbon and TechZone MCP servers. The hands-on build in the next chapter runs in mock mode and does not depend upon them.

This process is a relatively quick one, so long as you don't stray too far from the documentation. Do not attempt to install the CE Bob Marketplace via an Extensions search — you will come up empty handed. Follow the instructions as-written (below) in order to properly configure the environment.

docs.title: ii. Prerequisites
docs.text:
The illustration above serves as a one page map of the setup work ahead. Follow along in the subsequent steps for detailed, step-by-step guidance (with links and highlighted screen captures throughout.)

Ensure that you have each of the following prerequisites in hand before embarking on the lab setup. Two minutes of checks now will save you an hour of troubleshooting later.

BEFORE YOU BEGIN

  • Valid w3id credentials
  • Administrative rights to install software on your local machine
  • A Cisco AnyConnect VPN connection to the IBM Intranet
  • An account on github.ibm.com, or a personal GitHub account linked to the IBM GitHub organization (section iv, Step 2)

A GITHUB ACCOUNT IS REQUIRED

The CE Bob Marketplace catalog is served from the IBM GitHub (enterprise) organization. Without an account on github.ibm.com you cannot generate the personal access token that unlocks it. If you are unable to obtain access, you can still complete this lab. Download the Demo Builder as a packaged workspace from Seismic instead by following section iv of the Business Partners page, then return to section viii of this page to verify the workspace.

ALREADY HAVE IBM BOB?

If the Bob IDE is already installed and authenticated on your machine, skip section iii and jump ahead to section iv.

docs.title: iii. Internal registration
docs.text:
The Internal registration route is the appropriate one for IBM regular employees. It grants a general-purpose IBM Bob account tied to your w3id, which is all this lab requires.

PREMIUM PACKAGES

The IBM Bob Premium Packages (for i, for Z, and for Java) are requested by IBMers separately via https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/bob/addons. None of them are required for this lab.

  1. Begin at the Bob Enterprise Sales Assets page on IBM Technology Zone.

    Once there, click Technical Resources in the left sidebar.

  1. Click See it under the "Internal Bob Sign Up" tile.

  1. You will be redirected to a sign-up form. Enter all of the requested information and press Submit.

  1. Review your responses if you like, then confirm by clicking Submit once more in the pop-up window.

    There will be a "Thank you" pop-up that appears afterward — you can simply dismiss it.

  1. After submission, you will receive a confirmation email.

  1. At this point you will need to wait — as noted, approval typically takes at least 24 hours.

    Once approved, you will receive an email — follow the Download Bob hyperlink within it.

  1. The Download Bob link opens a Box folder containing download links for various operating systems. Locate the version appropriate for your OS and click it.

  1. Click the appropriate file within the folder.

  1. Click Download.

  1. Review the License Agreement, and if you accept its terms and conditions, toggle I accept the agreement and press Next.

  1. Continue through the GUI-based install process common to most desktop software — review the instructions on each Setup page to configure Bob to your liking, and press Next to proceed.

  1. Installation should take roughly 5–10 minutes.

  1. A completion pop-up appears.

    Tick Launch IBM Bob (if it is not already checked) and press Finish.

  1. IBM Bob opens. Click Log in to Bob.

  1. When prompted The extension IBM Bob wants to sign in using Bob., click Allow to launch a web browser for authentication.

    Log in within the browser using your IBMid and password - those which are linked to the IBM Bob account you registered for in the previous steps.

  1. A few additional prompts may arise before authentication can complete:

    • If asked "Do you want to allow this website to open IBM Bob?", click Yes
    • Wait until the web browser refreshes to read Authentication Successful! before closing the browser window
    • Return to the Bob IDE, which has now been successfully authenticated and connected to the IBM Bob service

With IBM Bob authenticated, continue to section iv to install the CE Bob Marketplace extension.

docs.title: iv. Install the CE Bob Marketplace extension
docs.text:
The work ahead proceeds in four phases:

  • Install the Marketplace extension (this section)
  • Create the GitHub PAT that authenticates it (section v)
  • Register your token with the extension (section vi)
  • Instantiate the Demo Builder within a new Project workspace (section vii)
Want to learn more about the CE Bob Marketplace extension?

Additional documentation is available from the IBM GitHub repository. Be aware that you will need to link your personal GitHub account to the IBM GitHub organization before you can access the repository (Step 2, below).

https://github.ibm.com/ClientEngineering/bob/tree/main/How-To/Bob-Marketplace

The IBM Client Engineering Bob Marketplace Extension currently supports two options for installing the extension within the Bob IDE: Automated (recommended option) and Manual.

For simplicity, this lab guide will follow the Automated installation procedure; however, documentation for the Manual approach is also available online.

  1. Ensure your machine is connected via a Cisco AnyConnect VPN to the IBM Intranet.

    Without a VPN or Intranet connection, the necessary extensions (such as the CE Bob Marketplace) will not display the necessary collections and many of the fields will be marked as unreachable or empty.

  1. Create an IBM GitHub account — or request to link your personal GitHub account to the IBM GitHub (enterprise) organization. This is a hard requirement: the personal access token created in section v cannot be generated without it.

    Personal accounts on GitHub will not be able to access repositories stored on the IBM GitHub (enterprise) organization without first requesting access. To link a personal GitHub account to the IBM GitHub organization, you will require valid IBMid credentials.

    • In order to request access, first visit the following website (ensure your VPN connection is active):

      https://gh-user-map.opensource.dal.app.cirrus.ibm.com

    • Under the Account Linking header, locate the IBM GitHub Enterprise tile

    • Click the blue Authenticate button and supply your IBMid credentials, as well as details about your personal GitHub account name
    • You may be emailed to join the IBM GitHub organization, if you were not previously a member. Please accept the invitation and await confirmation before attempting to log in.

    NOTE: Two-factor authentication (2FA) must be enabled under your GitHub security settings before you can join an IBM organization.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: UNABLE TO ACCESS GITHUB OR REQUEST ACCESS
    • If you are unable to access the IBM GitHub organization or request access, first make sure that your VPN connection is active.
    • If the problem persists, download the Demo Builder as a packaged workspace from Seismic instead — section iv of the Business Partners page — and then return to section viii of this page. All the necessary files and lab assets arrive as a ZIP folder, which bypasses the GitHub requirement entirely.

  1. To initiate the Automated install path, open the Bob IDE and click the Open Bob icon from the top of the interface (located just to the right of the top-center search bar). This will open the Agentic Sidebar along the right-side of the Bob IDE.

  1. Ensure that the Agent mode is active within the mode switch toggle.

  1. Select from the two options below according to your machine's operating system.

    Copy the command line string to your clipboard and then paste into the Agentic Sidebar session, hitting Enter to execute the task.

    LINUX / MAC 
    curl -fsSL https://s3.eu-de.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/bob-marketplace/marketplace-install-mac-linux.sh | bash
    WINDOWS 
    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "iwr https://s3.eu-de.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/bob-marketplace/marketplace-install-win.sh -UseBasicParsing | iex"

  1. Bob will pause at a Tools awaiting approval: checkpoint before running anything. In the documented run, Bob declined to pipe the installer straight into a shell. Instead, it proposed downloading the script to a temporary file and reading it in full before deciding whether to execute it.

    Review the proposed Execute Command and click Approve to let Bob retrieve the script.

    AGENTIC SIDEBAR OUTPUT

    I'll download the script and read it before running it, rather than piping it straight into bash.

$ curl -fsSL https://s3.eu-de.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/bob-marketplace/marketplace-install-mac-linux.sh -o /tmp/marketplace-install.sh && wc -l /tmp/marketplace-install.sh && cat /tmp/marketplace-install.sh
242 /tmp/marketplace-install.sh
#!/bin/bash
# Installer for the "Bob PreSales DEMO Builder Marketplace" Bob IDE extension.
# macOS / Linux. Designed to be pasted into Bob Chat (Advanced mode) and run.
#
# It downloads the extension VSIX from public IBM Cloud Object Storage
# (no API key required), unpacks it into Bob's user extensions folder, and
# registers it so Bob loads it on next launch.
#
# Usage:
#   curl -fsSL <this-script-url> | bash
#   ./marketplace-install-mac-linux.sh [--file <local.vsix>] [--url <vsix-url>]

    Bob's review of the script (roughly 240 lines in total) establishes two facts worth knowing before you approve its execution:

    • The script installs a Bob IDE extension and nothing else.
    • It reads your Bob login email from a local settings database and prints it to the terminal. It does not transmit the email anywhere.

  1. Bob also searches the IBM Bob documentation for guidance on installing Marketplace extensions by script. The documentation describes installation through the in-app Marketplace and a separate bob.ibm.com script for Bob Shell. It does not mention this installation route or the hosting bucket.

    The source should therefore be confirmed as trusted by the person running the installation. In this case, the source is a trusted (IBM Client Engineering) one, so this is simply an instance of Bob being vigilant against potential security threats.

    The Cloud Object Storage bucket hosting the installer is not an official bob.ibm.com location. Confirm that you trust where a link came from before approving any script's execution — a habit worth keeping well beyond this lab.

  1. Approve the Execute Command checkpoint for running the saved script. Bob executes it locally, and the script performs the following operations in order:

    OPERATION WHAT HAPPENS Environment check Verifies that Bob is installed by locating Bob's configuration directories under your home directory. Reports the Bob IDE version (for example 1.126.0+bob2.2.1) and the logged-in user email. Package download Retrieves the extension package (a .vsix file, which is a zip archive) from the public bucket. Confirms the file is a valid zip archive and not an error page. Extraction Unpacks the package into a temporary directory and reads the extension manifest to identify the publisher, name, and version. Installation Removes any earlier versions of the extension, then moves the new version into ~/.bobide/extensions/. Registration Adds an entry for the extension to ~/.bobide/extensions/extensions.json so that Bob loads it at startup.

    When finished, Bob reports that the Bob PreSales DEMO Builder Marketplace extension (ibm-ce.bob-marketplace, version 0.19.0 at the time of writing) has been installed.

    AGENTIC SIDEBAR OUTPUT

    The "Bob PreSales DEMO Builder Marketplace" extension (v0.19.0, ibm-ce.bob-marketplace) is installed. To use it, fully quit and reopen Bob, then look for "Bob Powers" in the sidebar. I haven't opened it, so I can't say whether it loads correctly.

    Bob did not inspect the contents of the extension itself, and it did not launch the extension to verify that it loads correctly. The script ran only the download and unpack operations described above. Verifying that the extension loads is a check you will perform yourself in the next two steps.

  1. Fully quit (completely close and exit) the Bob IDE, then restart the application. The extension registers at startup, so a full relaunch is required before it becomes visible.

  1. Look for CE Bob Marketplace in the Activity Bar (the left-hand icon strip). The extension contributes a view container titled CE Bob Marketplace. It activates automatically after startup, so it should be visible as soon as the Bob IDE finishes restarting.

    BOB POWERS?

    IBM Bob, while executing Steps 6 through 8 (above), may mistakenly refer to a "Bob Powers" extension. There is no such extension - it is a mislabeling of the correct "CE Bob Marketplace" extension. If you were to drill into questioning Bob about "what are Bob Powers?" you'll also find it arrives at the same conclusion: the extension you've installed, and the one that should be visible from the left-hand taskbar, is the "CE Bob Marketplace."

    TROUBLESHOOTING: PERMISSION CHECKS, WORKSPACE ERRORS, OR A MISSING TAB

    Your run may unfold differently from the one documented above. Participants running Bob for the first time have reported the following sequence instead, as Bob establishes the necessary permissions to access directories and folders on the local machine.

    • Bob prompts a Tools awaiting approval: checkpoint describing the Execute Command as one that downloads a shell script from a remote URL and pipes it directly into 'bash', executing code from an untrusted source. Toggle on the I understand the risk button to the right of the Security Warning prompt and click Approve to continue.

    • Bob may then return a Command failed complaint: The workspace directory doesn't exist yet, which is preventing the shell from starting. Let me run this from the home directory instead. Further down the session, another Execute Command approval request (this time for cwd .) will be pending. Check the I understand the risk toggle box and click Approve to continue.

    • A further Command failed prompt may follow, with an error similar to: The shell cannot start because the workspace directory /Users/.../.bob/playground does not exist on disk. Bob will suggest within the Agentic Sidebar a command that you can run directly within the Bob IDE Terminal. Be sure to use the one that Bob suggests for your machine.

      • Copy the command from the Agentic Sidebar chat to your clipboard
      • Open a new Terminal by clicking Terminal > New Terminal from the top menu bar (or by pressing Ctrl+Shift+` as a shortcut)
      • Paste the command into the Terminal console and hit Enter to execute

      After a moment, the Terminal console should report back that it has Installed Bob PreSales DEMO Builder Marketplace and that you should Fully quit and reopen Bob.. before continuing further. Quit and restart the Bob IDE to expose the newly-installed extension.

    • If, upon restarting, the CE Bob Marketplace tab is still not visible along the left-hand side: return to the Agentic Sidebar session. You can directly click on previous sessions within here to resume where you last left off.

      • Within the previous session's chat, enter the text Continue and hit Enter
      • Bob will likely report that The workspace directory now exists (since you're continuing), let me try the command again.
      • If prompted with an Execute Command checkpoint, check the I understand the risk box and click Approve to continue
      • Wait until Bob reports back a successful Installation complete summary
      • Exit and restart the Bob IDE once again to apply the changes

docs.title: v. Configure a personal access (GitHub API) token
docs.text:
The CE Bob Marketplace requires a valid GitHub Enterprise API Token in order to expose the Marketplace catalog contents. As mentioned previously, you will need to have linked your personal GitHub account to the IBM GitHub organization (section iv, Step 2) before you can access the IBM GitHub page.

  1. First, you'll want to generate a new Personal Access Token (PAT) — otherwise known as a GitHub Enterprise API Token.

    Open a web browser and navigate to the following website:

    https://github.ibm.com/settings/tokens/new

  1. Fill out the New personal access token (classic) request form according to the following (recommended) specifications to create a new Personal Access Token (PAT) that will serve as your GitHub Enterprise API Token.

    FIELD SET TO Note A unique name of your choosing Expiration 90 days Scopes Check the repo option (all subitems under repo will automatically be enabled)

    All other fields should remain off (their default values). When ready, scroll down to the bottom of the page and click Generate token to proceed.

  1. Copy the PAT to your clipboard and save it to a notepad for future reference. You will not be able to look up the key once you have navigated away from this screen, but you can always regenerate a new one in future if needed.

docs.title: vi. Authenticate the CE Bob Marketplace extension
docs.text:
With your PAT / GitHub Enterprise API Token in hand, it's time to authenticate the extension within the Bob IDE.

  1. From the relaunched Bob IDE, click the newly-installed CE Bob Marketplace tab from the left-hand side of the interface. Double-check that your VPN connection is active.

  1. Click the key icon labelled Bob Marketplace: Set Repository Token within the CE Bob Marketplace tab. This will automatically open the top-center prompt window.

  1. The prompt window is awaiting a decision to Set token for which repository? with drop-down menu appearing below with various options you can choose from.

    Click (or use your keyboard up and down arrows to highlight, followed by Enter) the https://github.ibm.com/ClientEngineering/bob option.

  1. Next you will be asked to provide the personal access token recorded in section v, Step 3.

    Paste the token into the context window and press Enter to confirm.

Once fully authenticated and authorized, the CE Bob Marketplace tab will render a complete inventory of available assets such as:

  • Collections
  • Modes
  • Skills
  • Rules
  • MCP
  • Labs
  • Recipes & guides

In order to validate that your environment is fully authenticated, click into any of the categories mentioned above. There should be a substantial number of assets under each category — with these lists (and categories, most likely) expected to grow over time.

With the Marketplace installed, it's now time to prepare and configure the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder.

docs.title: vii. Install the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder collection
docs.text:
Among the Collections available on the CE Bob Marketplace is the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder collection, which provides one-click setup for building credible IBM-grade demos quickly and is the primary focus of this hands-on lab. This will be the tool that you use to rapidly craft IBM product demonstrations, stay on-message with your client demo, and drastically cut down on preparation time ahead of every client engagement.

  1. From the Bob IDE, click into the Explorer tab and then select Open Folder.

  1. Create a New Folder on your local machine in a directory of your choosing.

    • Name the directory something recognizable, such as Bob Demo Builder
    • When ready, click Create to finalize the new directory
    • If the Bob IDE has not automatically opened the Bob Demo Builder directory, click File > Open Folder... from the top menu bar and then select the new directory.

    Open the newly-created folder to expose its contents (which at this time are empty) within the Explorer tab.

    RESTRICTED MODE

    When opening a new directory, the Bob IDE may automatically enable Restricted Mode which will lock-out extensions (like the CE Bob Marketplace) and executables from access until such restrictions are lifted.

    If you are unable to locate the CE Bob Marketplace tab along the left-hand side of the Bob IDE interface, look for a blue highlighted Restricted Mode shield icon in the bottom-left corner of the IDE.

    To remove the restrictions and expose the CE Bob Marketplace tab:

    • Click the Restricted Mode button to pull open the configuration screen
    • Examine the two options under the You are in Restricted Mode panel: In a Trusted Folder and In Restricted Mode
    • Click the Trust button under the In a Trusted Folder option to disable restrictions
    • Click the X icon in the top-right corner of the panel to return to the main Bob IDE dashboard

    With the Restricted Mode limitations disabled, the CE Bob Marketplace button should be restored to the left-hand tabs of the Bob IDE.

  1. Click the newly-exposed CE Bob Marketplace tab from the left-hand side of the Bob IDE interface.

  1. At the top of the panel is a search bar. Enter the following to filter from the various collections and assets:

    IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder

  1. Click the Install button next to the item that exactly matches the search filter. Note that there are multiple Pre-Sales Demo Builders available (...for Automation, ...for Java, etc.) in the Marketplace.

    For the purposes of this hands-on lab, you will be utilizing the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder collection only.

  1. When prompted Install 10 items from IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder?, confirm by clicking Install.

    Wait for the Installing... icon to switch back to Install before advancing to the next step. This is a misleading quirk of the UI, we know. Installation time is approximately 1 minute.

  1. To verify that the collection has been installed, click the Explorer tab once again.

    • Examine the contents of the Bob Demo Builder folder, which should now contain a .bob directory
    • Click the > arrow to the left of .bob to expand the directory contents: rules, skills, mcp.json

    These directories contain all of the components needed to complete this hands-on lab and demo-builder exercises.

To summarize your work so far, at this stage you have:

  • Installed the CE Bob Marketplace
  • Created a GitHub personal access token and linked it to the Marketplace
  • Installed the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder collection

Continue to section viii to verify the workspace.

docs.title: viii. Verify the workspace
docs.text:
Before any demo work begins, confirm that the workspace is trusted and that the Demo Builder mode is available to the Agentic Sidebar.

  1. Check the bottom-left corner of the IDE for a blue Restricted Mode shield icon. If it is showing, the workspace has been opened in Restricted Mode and the Demo Builder's assets will not load. Click the shield and choose Trust under the In a Trusted Folder option, exactly as described in section vii, Step 2.
  1. Within the Explorer tab, confirm that the Bob Demo Builder folder contains a .bob directory. Expand it to find rules, skills, and mcp.json.

  1. Open the Agentic Sidebar (click the Open Bob icon at the top of the interface) and click the mode selector button to expand the list of available modes. You will find IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder loaded and ready to use.

    Leave the mode set to Agent for now. You will switch into the Demo Builder mode at the start of the next chapter.

READINESS CHECK

Before proceeding, verify each of the following items:

  • Client Engineering Bob Marketplace icon is visible
  • GitHub API token is configured
  • Marketplace catalog loads successfully and its Modes and Skills (as well as its MCP servers) are visible
  • The workspace is trusted (no Restricted Mode shield in the bottom-left corner)
  • The workspace contains a .bob directory with rules, skills, and mcp.json
  • The IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode is listed within the Agentic Sidebar's mode selector

A WORD ON WORKING WITH GENERATIVE AI

IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most developers are accustomed to. In practice, that means the same prompt can produce different code from one run to the next. This is both a strength and a quirk of the technology, and it is something to work with rather than against.

Precision is what tips the odds in your favor. The more clearly you describe what you want, the more closely Bob's output will mirror your intent; conversely, the smallest change in wording can meaningfully change the generated code. Throughout this lab, your results may differ from the solutions shown — and that is expected, not a defect. Whenever an output diverges, you have three good options: refine the prompt and try again, edit the generated code by hand, or simply proceed if the variation still compiles and runs. Human review remains essential at every step, and never more so than while you are still learning the tool.

docs.title: ix. Optional: Connect the Carbon and TechZone MCP servers
docs.text:
The Demo Builder collection references two MCP servers:

  • Carbon (IBM's design system)
  • TechZone (environment provisioning and documentation)

This section is optional. The mock-mode build documented in the next chapter completes without either server configured — the Business Partner route has always been built that way. Configure them now if you intend to take the Demo Builder beyond this lab into live builds and client environments; otherwise, skip ahead to section x.

Each server requires short-lived credentials for access — three in total, which you (the user) will gather in the steps ahead and store within a separate document (such as Notepad) for later use:

CREDENTIAL ACQUIRED FROM Carbon Authorization Code The Carbon MCP IBMid flow (detailed in the steps below) Carbon Session ID The Carbon MCP IBMid flow (generated alongside the Authorization Code) TechZone API token Your TechZone profile page (detailed in the steps below)

  1. To create your Carbon MCP authorizations, navigate to the following website using your web browser:

    https://carbondesignsystem.com/developing/carbon-mcp/onboarding-and-setup/

  1. Scroll down to the Token and session ID section of the page.

    Click the Generate a token and session ID button to open a new tab.

  1. The web browser will be redirected to the usual IBM sign-in page. Authenticate with your IBMid credentials.

docs.text:
READINESS CHECK

Before proceeding, verify each of the following items:

  • The workspace is trusted (no Restricted Mode shield in the bottom-left corner)
  • The workspace contains a .bob directory with rules, skills, and mcp.json
  • The IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode is listed within the Agentic Sidebar's mode selector
  • Internal registration grants a general-purpose IBM Bob account tied to your w3id. Approval takes 24+ hours, and the Premium Packages are requested separately (they play no part in this lab).

docs.title: i. Overview
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Business Partner pathway for the Bob Demo Builder hands-on enablement. [3 min]

This page is written for IBM Business Partners. IBM regular employees should follow the companion page, IBMers | Setup and registration, which registers internally and installs the Demo Builder from the Client Engineering Bob Marketplace.

The Business Partner route is fully self-contained. The internal CE Bob Marketplace, the GitHub personal access token, and the MCP credentials that IBMers configure are not required here. Within this chapter, you will assemble the Bob Demo-Builder environment in three stages:

  • Register for IBM Bob by requesting an IBM Bob Enterprise entitlement through IBM Technology Zone, then authenticate the Bob IDE on your local machine
  • Download the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder as a packaged workspace from IBM Seismic: the Mode together with its Skills, Rules and MCP configuration — pre-loaded and ready to open
  • Verify the workspace, so that the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode is available within the Agentic Sidebar before any demo work begins

Both routes arrive at the same working demonstration in the next chapter.

docs.title: ii. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure that you have each of the following prerequisites in hand before embarking on the lab setup. Two minutes of checks now will save you an hour of troubleshooting later.

BEFORE YOU BEGIN

  • Valid IBMid credentials (the same IBMid you use to sign in to IBM Technology Zone)
  • Administrative rights to install software on your local machine
  • Access to IBM Seismic for the packaged download in section iv

No Intranet or VPN connection is required.

ALREADY HAVE IBM BOB?

If the Bob IDE is already installed and authenticated on your machine (through a Free Trial account, for example), skip section iii and jump ahead to section iv. Any authenticated IBM Bob account can run the Demo Builder.

docs.title: iii. Request an IBM Bob Enterprise entitlement
docs.text:

  1. Requests for IBM Bob Enterprise entitlements are made via IBM Technology Zone. Visit the following collection to begin the process:

    URL: https://techzone.ibm.com/collection/bob-business-partner-enablement/environments

    From the left-hand side of the page, click the Environments tab.

  1. Four options will be available:

    • Request entitlement for IBM Bob Enterprise
    • Request entitlement for IBM Bob Premium Package for i
    • Request entitlement for IBM Bob Premium Package for Z

    Click the Reserve it button below the Request entitlement for IBM Bob Enterprise tile.

  1. Step 1: General of the configuration process will ask you to specify a Name and Description for your reservation. When ready, click Next in the bottom-right corner to continue.

If you mistakenly click the wrong option, or if the reservation system does not allow you to continue without an opportunity number, exit out from this page and try again (making sure to only click Test). When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 3: Deployment will ask you to specify the Geography for your deployment. Select the data center location that is closest to you. When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 4: Scheduling will ask you to specify the go-live and termination dates for your entitlement. Choose a window that comfortably covers the time you expect to spend on this lab. If the entitlement lapses before you finish, you can submit a new request using these same instructions. When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 6: Review and submit will ask you to review your configuration settings before submitting the request. Scroll down through your reservation details and, if you approve, check the I agree to IBM Technology Zone's terms & conditions and user security policies. box at the bottom of the page. When ready, click Submit to initiate the reservation request.

  1. The web browser will redirect automatically to IBM Technology Zone's My requests dashboard. From this page, you can monitor and track the progression of your reservation request as it moves from Scheduled to Provisioning to Ready. Wait until the request is marked as Ready before advancing.

    Average deployment times are roughly 5 minutes or less.

  1. When the reservation is Ready, you will receive an email to your inbox providing you with a link to the environment and the same details will also be accessible via the My requests dashboard (where you were tracking the reservation request).

    Click either the View your request link in the email body OR click the arrow to the left of your reservation name on the My requests dashboard to expand details about the request.

  1. Both links will direct to the IBM Bob dashboard:

    URL: https://bob.ibm.com/admin

    If you previously registered for IBM Bob by another route (such as a Free Trial), the default option below this may display text such as Free Trial or something else entirely.

    • Click the box below Choose workspace to open a drop-down menu
    • Your request via IBM Technology Zone will have added a new option to this list, similar to TECHZONE-BobathonV2 (us-east): this is your newly-provisioned IBM Bob Enterprise entitlement
    • Select the TECHZONE-... option as your workspace and then continue with the login

    EXACT WORDING VARIES BY REGION

    The label of the workspace depends on the geography you selected in Step 5 and may not read exactly as it does in the screen capture. Look for the option prefixed with TECHZONE.

  1. The web browser will automatically load into the IBM Bob dashboard.

    • Verify in the top-left corner that the TECHZONE-... workspace is selected for Organization
    • Click the Subscription tab to view your plan type and seat count, as well as your Bobcoin balance

  1. If the Bob IDE is not yet installed on your machine, download and install it now. Select the version that matches your operating system.

  1. Open the Bob IDE and press Log in to Bob.

  1. Press Allow on the pop-up window, followed by Open on the subsequent pop-up window.

  1. On the IBM Verify sign-in page, expand the "Choose an option" drop-down and press IBMid. Sign in with the same IBMid that you used on IBM Technology Zone.

  1. You should be redirected to an "Authentication Successful!" screen.

    Afterward, return to the tab with IBM Bob open and press Open on the new window that has appeared on the IBM Bob screen. Look to the Agentic Sidebar — the window for entering prompts has opened. You have now successfully accessed your authenticated IBM Bob account.

  1. One last check binds the IDE to your entitlement. Look towards the bottom-right corner of the Bob IDE interface. Along the bottom edge of the interface there will be an interactable button labelled Bob Settings — click this button to open the Settings panel.

docs.text:
READINESS CHECK

Before proceeding, verify each of the following items:

docs.title: 2. Deploying with demo builder
docs.text: BOB DEMO-BUILDER MODE

docs.title: i. From concept to demo
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of deploying with the Bob Demo Builder hands-on enablement. [3 min]

Before continuing, a brief recap on where things stand and the work you've carried out so far:

PRE-REQUISITES

  1. IBM Bob is installed and authenticated (Chapter 1 — the Setup page for your audience)

  2. The IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder is in place within your workspace — installed from the CE Bob Marketplace (IBMers) or unpacked from the Seismic package (Business Partners)

  3. The workspace has been verified and the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode is visible within the Agentic Sidebar

Now it's time to put this preparation into practice. In the chapter ahead, you will take a one-sentence use case — an AI agent that watches factory equipment and heads off failures before they occur — and carry it through the Demo Builder's full lifecycle:

TO-DO'S

  1. Guided intake

  2. Autonomous build

  3. Local launch

  4. One-click quickstart script

  5. Review-and-refine pass

  6. Client-ready demo script

The flow documented could be described as a "simplified" example and it's been intentionally designed as such to minimize the complexity of your first hands-on experience with this process. It also keeps the Bob tokens consumption to a minimum. For those wanting a more elaborate and resource-intensive example, you will have the opportunity to practice this in the chapters ahead.

For now, with the simplified example of this chapter, you will build in mock mode. This approach requires zero credentials and works fully offline. There is no watsonx.ai environment to provision and no API key to supply; the workspace you configured in the previous chapter is all that is needed. The purpose is to experience the complete arc of the Demo Builder methodology end-to-end, and to establish repeatable patterns that you can apply (with fuller briefs and real environments) to potential client opportunities at a later time.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
The division of labor in this chapter is the discipline this course has been reinforcing from the beginning: Bob does the building; the human-in-the-loop (you) makes the final decisions and calls the shots. The intake questions that the Demo Builder poses at the start are critical decision points that you must answer:

  • The build approach
  • The environment
  • The deployment target
  • The industry scenario

Once those decisions have been recorded and sanctioned, Bob executes those instructions autonomously. It generates the code and then verifies and tests it. As you will witness first-hand, it also catches and repairs its own bugs along the way. Throughout this process you maintain your role as the principal arbiter: approving additional actions and validating the results, then advancing (or re-orienting) the workflow.

There is a second lesson embedded here as well. Despite "mock mode" having no live models or real environments backing it, the finalized demonstration is a complete and navigable Carbon-styled application. It ships with preset AI scenarios and a results view. It includes an architecture view and a generated walkthrough script. For engagements where you are short on time (or short on Bob tokens before the month rolls over), these types of lightweight demonstrations can be immensely valuable in a pinch.

Finally, there is a practical dimension worth internalizing. The full build consumes roughly 20 minutes of time and approximately 15–20 Bobcoins. For a Business Partner especially, that means a credible IBM demonstration no longer requires provisioned environments or weeks of scarce technical talent as its price of admission.

docs.title: iii. Briefing the demo builder
docs.text:
A WORD ON WORKING WITH GENERATIVE AI

IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most developers are accustomed to. In practice, that means the same prompt can produce different code from one run to the next. This is both a strength and a quirk of the technology, and it is something to work with rather than against.

Precision is what tips the odds in your favor. The more clearly you describe what you want, the more closely Bob's output will mirror your intent; conversely, the smallest change in wording can meaningfully change the generated code. Throughout this lab, your results may differ from the solutions shown — and that is expected, not a defect. Whenever an output diverges, you have three good options: refine the prompt and try again, edit the generated code by hand, or simply proceed if the variation still compiles and runs. Human review remains essential at every step, and never more so than while you are still learning the tool.

The first stage of any Demo Builder engagement is switching into the correct mode and handing Bob a one-sentence use case. From there, Bob will run pre-flight checks and walk you through a short guided intake, where each of Bob's questions is a decision point you must answer.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, click the Modes selector (which is likely displaying Agent mode at this time) to expose more options:

  1. From the drop-down list, switch to the IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode.

  1. With IBM Bob now in IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode, paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar and press Enter to execute.

    I need a demo of an AI agent that monitors IoT sensor data from factory equipment, predicts failures before they happen, and automatically creates maintenance work orders with recommended parts and technicians.

  1. IBM Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode will first run pre-flight checks to ensure everything is prepared and then begins the intake process.

    • Approve the MCP tool prompt
    • Click the Approve for task toggle to reduce the amount of manual approvals required later in the flow

    In the Business Partner run, no MCP tool prompt appeared at this stage and Bob moved directly into the intake questions. If that is what you see, simply carry on.

SEQUENCING THE INTAKE

In the steps ahead, you will answer a short series of intake questions that shape the build. Each decision determines a different facet of your finished demo, from the technology stack and environment mode through to the deployment target and industry scenario. The exact set (and order) of questions varies from one run to the next: the two documented runs between them produced the seven decision points described below. Treat any question your run skips as a decision Bob has made for you — and review it at the final confirmation.

Intake 1: Build Approach

Bob asks how the AI agent should be built. This selection determines whether the demo uses watsonx.ai (a LangGraph ReAct agent running in a FastAPI backend) or one of the alternative build approaches, such as watsonx Orchestrate. For this walkthrough, choose the watsonx.ai option.

  1. Once the pre-flight checks are completed, the Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode will present a short sequence of questions in order to tailor the demo to your requirements.

    First, it asks "How should the AI agent be built? [...]". Select the top option:

    watsonx.ai (RECOMMENDED) — A LangGraph ReAct agent running in a FastAPI backend.

    YOUR OPTIONS WILL LIKELY DIFFER

    The exact options presented will very likely be different in your run — the key is simply to select the option carrying watsonx.ai. In the Business Partner run, for example, the same choice was labelled as follows:

    "Use suggestion: watsonx.ai App demo (RECOMMENDED) — LangGraph ReAct agent in FastAPI, Carbon dashboard with real-time sensor charts, anomaly det..."

    The watsonx Orchestrate demo setup is more advanced; additional details can be found here: https://github.ibm.com/ClientEngineering/bob/blob/main/Pre-Sales-Demo-Builder/Sample-Reciepies/07-Predictive-Maintenance-Agent.md

Intake 2: Target Audience

Bob may ask who the demonstration will be presented to. This selection tailors the framing, level of detail, and pitch length. For this walkthrough, the specific choice does not impact the build.

  1. Next, you may be asked what audience the demonstration should be presented to. This question surfaced in the Business Partner run and was skipped in the IBMer run.

    The selection does not particularly matter for this exercise — here, we chose: "C-suite / VP of Operations / Plant Director — 15-minute executive overview [...]"

Intake 3: Environment Mode

Bob asks whether you have a live watsonx.ai environment provisioned. In real engagements, live API keys can be provided to power genuine model responses. For this walkthrough, you will use mock mode, which produces impressive results with zero credentials and works fully offline.

  1. Next, Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode asks whether you already have a watsonx.ai environment provisioned.

    THIS SELECTION IS CRUCIAL

    Select: "No — build in mock mode only (zero credentials needed, works fully offline)" — or whichever option in your run carries mock mode only.

    In a future section, you will explore how this mode operates when an environment actually is provisioned. For now, mock mode presents the complete overview of the capabilities — with none of the credential overhead. As you will see, realistic and impressive results are achievable even upon purely synthetic data.

Intake 4: Deployment Target

Bob asks how the app should be deployed. Selecting the run locally option ensures the demo can be launched from your machine without Docker or Podman — the simplest path for a client meeting.

  1. Next, you are asked "How do you want to run and deploy this demo".

    Select the "Run locally" option that fits your specific operating system — typically one of the top two responses. For example:

    Run locally first — I'm on Intel/AMD (amd64) Mac, Linux, or Windows

    SELECT THE LOCAL OPTION

    The wording on your options is likely different. In the Business Partner run it read "Use suggestion: Run locally first (RECOMMENDED default) [...]". The key is to select the run local option and to avoid Docker or Podman.

Intake 5: Industry Scenario

Bob may ask which specific factory equipment scenario should be showcased. This selection defines the demo's narrative — the equipment types, the sensor data, and the failure modes that will drive the walkthrough. For this walkthrough, choose the industrial CNC/conveyor/HVAC scenario.

  1. Next, it may ask "What specific factory equipment scenario should be showcased?" This question surfaced in the IBMer run and was skipped in the Business Partner run.

    Click the top option:

    Industrial CNC machines + conveyor belts + HVAC systems \[...\]

    Here you have more flexibility. If a listed industry or scenario aligns better with your own experience or interests, you are welcome to select it. However, in practice your results may drift further from the captures shown in this guide should you opt to do so.

Intake 6: Final Confirmation

Bob asks for a final confirmation that the recorded intake selections are correct. Approving here commits the plan and hands execution over to Bob for the autonomous build.

  1. Finally, Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode requests a final confirmation that everything is in order.

    Select the following option to conclude the fact-gathering phase and move ahead with the build instructions:

    No — we have everything, start building now!

    In the Business Partner run, the equivalent option read "No - proceed with the build [...]". Whatever the wording, select the option that allows the build to proceed.

Intake 7: Auto-Approve Permissions

Before the build begins, decide how much autonomy Bob receives. Enabling Auto-approve eliminates repetitive clicking during the 20-minute build, at the cost of stepping back from each individual action.

  1. With every question answered, consider the Auto-approve Permissions you wish to grant Bob. Press the Shield (Permissions) icon next to the mode selector to open these settings.

    For ease of use, and to avoid repetitive clicking, the Business Partner run enabled Auto-approve and toggled all permissions on. The IBMer run left auto-approve off and relied on Approve for task at each checkpoint instead; the steps ahead document that run.

    CONSIDER THE CONTROL YOU HAND OVER

    Weigh the level of control you are comfortable delegating to IBM Bob. If auto-approvals sit uneasily with you, this flow can be completed perfectly well with every auto-approval disabled and purely manual approvals. You will simply need to click "Approve" or "Approve for Task" quite a few more times throughout the lab.

docs.title: iv. The autonomous build
docs.text:
With the intake complete, the balance of the work shifts to Bob. Your role across the following steps encompasses oversight and steering: review what Bob proposes and either approve the workflow or course-correct as necessary.

Bob will execute the build across the following (or similar) sub-tasks:

TASK OBJECTIVES Sub-Task 1 Scaffold project subdirectories Sub-Task 2 Build the back-end Sub-Task 3 Run back-end verification Sub-Task 4 Run back-end tests Sub-Task 5 Build the front-end Sub-Task 6 Run final compliance tests

In the Business Partner run, Bob organized the same work as a 5-step build plan: scaffold and environment setup; a synthetic data generator; the back-end (FastAPI + LangGraph agent); the front-end (Carbon React, 5 pages); and Docker/scripts/docs. Sub-Task 1: Initial Kickoff and Scaffolding

Bob confirms the intake decisions and begins scaffolding the project. This includes creating the subdirectories that will store the front-end and back-end, along with the data and documentation for the demo.

Sub-Task 2: Build the Back-End

Bob creates the subdirectories and begins generating the back-end files: the configuration and the FastAPI service first, then the LangGraph agent and the synthetic data layer.

    Click Approve for task once again.

With the back-end deployed and validated, Bob moves on to the front-end. It generates a full Vite + React application using IBM's Carbon Design System. The pages cover the AI agent and its results view, as well as the architecture diagram.

      Click Approve for task.

    SELF-REVIEW IN ACTION: THE CARBON ICON SWEEP (BUSINESS PARTNER RUN)

In the Business Partner run, Bob finished generating all files and then identified a known Carbon icon compatibility problem: some @carbon/react Sass imports and icon names needed to be validated against the Carbon v11 specification before the app could build cleanly. With auto-approve enabled, the entire repair unfolded without a single click.

    The icon sweep continued with targeted diffs to ProblemPage.jsx and SolutionPage.jsx as well as App.jsx. These replaced any icon references that may not exist in Carbon v11 with known-safe alternatives.

Uncertain names were replaced with confirmed safe alternatives such as BarChart and Document. At this stage, 42 files had been updated and modified.

docs.title: v. Launch the demo
docs.text:
With the build complete and verified, the next stage is to launch the demo locally. This is a two-terminal sequence: one for the FastAPI back-end, and one for the Vite front-end. Bob provides the exact commands in its final completion message. If something breaks along the way, the recommended remedy is to paste the console log directly into the Agentic Sidebar and let Bob diagnose the issue.

  1. At this stage, the demo build has been completed and verified.

    Read through the final completion message and locate the Terminal commands (documented within the console read-out) to start the application.

    In the Business Partner run, the same information was presented under a "To Start Now" section of the build summary. That build consumed approximately 15 Bobcoins and modified 42 files.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: THE STARTUP COMMANDS DO NOT WORK

    Occasionally, the startup steps you initially receive for your app may not work. Whether it proves a simple syntax issue or a larger problem, getting past it is simple enough. Tell IBM Bob in natural language that there is an error and paste the entire console log.

    When an error surfaces, Bob will find a solution quickly. If the provided solution does not work on the first attempt, keep iterating in the same fashion: simply copy and paste the console output into the Agentic Sidebar.

    Bob will then provide new commands to start the app. The commands you receive will probably differ from those documented here. What is likely to remain consistent is that you will work in two separate Terminal windows, one each for the back-end and the front-end.

  1. Launch a new Terminal within the Bob IDE by clicking Terminal > New Terminal from the top-line menu bar.

  1. Copy the Terminal 1 - Backend command line string (from Step 18) to your clipboard, paste it into the new Terminal console, and hit Enter to execute.

    Execute these instructions line by line, one at a time.

    Continue executing each instruction from Terminal 1 - Backend until the service has successfully started.

    WHAT THE BACK-END COMMANDS TYPICALLY LOOK LIKE (BUSINESS PARTNER RUN)

    The first back-end command changes into the back-end directory. In this example, that meant a cd into demos/new-demo/backend. Your path will reflect your own machine's Downloads location.

    The second back-end command activates the Python virtual environment: .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 on Windows. Once active, your Terminal prompt will show (venv) to confirm that the environment is ready.

    The final back-end command starts the service: uvicorn main:app --reload --port 8000. You should see Uvicorn report that it is running on http://127.0.0.1:8000, confirming the FastAPI backend is live and watching for changes.

  1. With the back-end service successfully started, you will need to open a second Terminal console to run the front-end service.

    As before, click Terminal > New Terminal from the top-line menu of the Bob IDE. (Alternatively, click the + button to open a new Terminal window.)

  1. Copy the Terminal 2 - Frontend command line string (from Step 18) to your clipboard, paste it into the new Terminal console, and hit Enter to execute.

    Execute these instructions line by line, one at a time.

    Continue executing each instruction from Terminal 2 - Frontend until the service has successfully started.

    WHAT THE FRONT-END COMMANDS TYPICALLY LOOK LIKE (BUSINESS PARTNER RUN)

    The first front-end command changes into the front-end directory: a cd into demos/new-demo/frontend.

    Running npm install then installs all front-end dependencies. You should see output confirming that packages were audited with no vulnerabilities.

  1. To finish starting up the app, the final instruction to be executed within the Terminal console should resemble something like the following:

    npm run dev

    When it finishes, you will see a Local: http://localhost:5173/ (or similar port) link within the terminal output. This is the URL for your demo app.

  1. If successful, the Terminal console should report back that the app has started.

    Hold Ctrl and then left-click the URL to open the address embedded within the Terminal console to view the application with your default web browser.

    A WHITE SCREEN ON FIRST LOAD

    Upon accessing the site, you may initially see a white screen. Wait 1–2 minutes for the site to load. If the white screen persists, refresh or switch browsers. If the issue still persists, take a screenshot and describe the issue to Bob in the Agentic Sidebar.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: A STUCK SIDEBAR PANEL

    Notice any issues once the demo loads? Fixing them is simple: take a screenshot and send it to IBM Bob. In the Business Partner run, the sidebar panel was stuck.

    Simply describe the issue in natural language — providing a screenshot where possible — and Bob will fix it.

    Solve any issues you may experience with your app (a complete crash, poor aesthetics, and so on) in a similar fashion: describe the problem in natural language and provide screenshots.

docs.title: vi. The one-click quickstart script
docs.text:
The two-terminal startup sequence works, but it is not what you want to be running in front of a client. The next stage condenses the entire launch into a single double-click by asking Bob to generate a quickstart script. Remember that IBM Bob is remarkably flexible: if something is unclear to you at any point in the process, simply explain it to Bob in natural language.

  1. To avoid the manual startup sequence in the future, simply ask Bob to make a quickstart script, like so:

    Create a quickstart script so I can start my demo in one click, no terminal windows

    The wording is yours to choose. The IBMer run asked for the same thing as follows, with the same result:

    Make a quickstart script that allows me to start the app in 1 click, no manual Terminal windows.

  1. Bob will generate the script.

    To locate it quickly on your local machine, right-click any of the files on the IBM Bob sidebar and press "Reveal in File Explorer".

  1. Inspect the contents of the /IBM-Pre-Sales-Demo-Builder/ directory (or, for IBMers, your Bob Demo Builder workspace) and drill down into the /demos/ sub-directory.

  1. Within the /demos directory you should see a newly-created /new-demo subdirectory. Double-click it to expose the contents.

  1. In this example, IBM Bob created a script called START_DEMO.bat for a Windows machine. The file name and type you receive will differ, though the naming will likely be similar. Look for something carrying START or similar.

  1. Run (double-click) the demo script .BAT file.

    TROUBLESHOOTING

    Here, some of the Terminal windows that open appear troublesome, with error logs — but Bob built in fallbacks to address this. If your quickstart script crashes, take a screenshot (or copy and paste the console output) and send it to Bob.

  1. The quickstart script continues. You may experience completely different behaviour.

    Expect multiple Terminal windows to open. Do not close them. Leave them running while you access the demo app.

  1. Another demo script window opens. Depending on how your quickstart script is wired, the app may open automatically or you may need to click it yourself.

    • Look for a line reading http://localhost:517x/..., then hold Ctrl and click it
    • In this specific example, the app started on port 5175, since other ports were already in use
    • On a fresh run-through, your app will typically sit at http://localhost:5173

docs.title: vii. Explore and refine
docs.text:
A demo is only client-ready once you have actually clicked through it end-to-end. The next stage walks through the pages of the running app, exercises the AI analysis flow and the auto-generated work order feature, and demonstrates how to apply the screenshot + natural-language prompt pattern to fix any issues you encounter.

  1. Once the application has loaded within the web browser, begin investigating the various components and features to verify that everything works as expected. Click and scroll around, exploring the app to make sure no bugs are lurking.

    Keep in mind that your page may look somewhat (or very) different from the app documented here, owing to generative AI's non-deterministic properties.

  1. What happens when you press Run AI Agent? Open the tab to investigate.

  1. In this instance, the AI Analysis executes for the CRITICAL Bearing Failure Alert scenario.

    Proceed to the Results tab.

  1. Everything looks in order here. Continue by clicking Architecture.

  1. The Business Partner run produced an AI Agent page built around a scenario picker rather than a single alert. Return to the AI Agent and select one of the scenarios — here, the CNC Spindle Bearing Wear scenario.

Simply take a screenshot of your application as it is rendered within the web browser, paste that screenshot into the Agentic Sidebar as a reference for comparison, and then request the changes via a natural language prompt that describes the issue.

docs.title: viii. Pitching the demo script
docs.text:
A running app is only half of what the Demo Builder produces. The other half is a fully-authored DEMO_SCRIPT.md file containing a preflight checklist and a verbal walkthrough — the material you will actually present in the room.

  1. To conclude the simplified flow demonstration, one task remains: how do you actually work with (and pitch) this demo for a potential client audience?

    Back within the IBM Bob IDE, locate the Markdown file named DEMO_SCRIPT.md (or something similar) under the Explorer tab. It contains a set of pre-flight checks, alongside the actual demo script you could adapt for walking a prospective client end-to-end through this demonstration. Of course, you can also use the Agentic Sidebar at any time to request for Bob to generate a presentation script for you, bulleted and timed for exactly the length of time you'll have for your client engagement.

  1. In the Business Partner run, the file sat inside the /demos folder. Look inside it for a Markdown file named something similar to DEMO_SCRIPT.md — click on it.

  1. Right-click and press "Open Preview" within IBM Bob to see a formatted version of the script.

  1. Finally, observe that IBM Bob's Pre-Sales Demo Builder mode created an accompanying preflight checklist and verbal presentation script to sit alongside your demo app. To modify it, simply describe the desired changes to Bob.
